messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi's Case

Kofi was thirty-three when he returned from the Sahel, though sometimes he felt decades older. For eighteen months he had worked as a relief coordinator for an international NGO, moving between three countries to document displacement camps and facilitate aid distribution. The work had felt sacred to him—a way to transform the helplessness he'd carried since childhood into something purposeful. Then came the ambush.

It happened on a routine supply run to a camp outside a town whose name he now tried not to think. The convoy was flagged down by men in mismatched uniforms. Kofi was in the second vehicle. What followed was a blur of shouting in languages he half-understood, hands forcing him and two colleagues into the dust, the metallic click of rifle bolts, the sensation of his own breath becoming foreign in his chest. For four hours they were held at gunpoint while the men looted the medical supplies and fuel. One of Kofi's colleagues, a young woman named Amara, was separated from the group. When she returned, her shirt was torn and her eyes had gone flat. The men left without explanation. No ransom was demanded. No demands were made. They simply vanished into the landscape as if the violence had been arbitrary, motiveless—a fact of the terrain rather than a crime.

Back in the States, Kofi had expected the memories to fade. They did not. What gnawed at him most was the absence of consequence. The men were never identified. No investigation yielded names. The NGO filed reports that disappeared into bureaucratic channels. Amara had left the organization within weeks, and Kofi had heard through intermediaries that she'd moved back home, that she wasn't answering calls. The injustice of it had calcified into something harder than anger—a conviction that the world operated without accountability, that violence could be committed with impunity, that he had been powerless to stop it and remained powerless still. He had come to believe he could not trust his own judgment anymore; he had walked into that ambush, had not seen the danger coming, had failed to protect Amara. What kind of person, what kind of man, failed at that?

The certainty that danger was imminent and that he himself was unreliable began to reshape his days. At home in Atlanta, in the apartment he shared with his wife Zainab, Kofi found himself constantly monitoring. When they sat in the living room, he positioned himself with sight lines to both windows and the door. He scanned the street from behind the curtains before leaving the house. In grocery stores, he tracked the movements of other shoppers, noting exits, assessing threat. His body remained in a state of coiled readiness—his heart would surge at sudden noises, his shoulders would jolt at unexpected touches. Zainab had learned not to approach him from behind.

The hypervigilance was exhausting, and Kofi began trying to manage it by simply not thinking about what had happened. He would push the memories away when they surfaced, forcing his attention elsewhere. But the act of suppressing them seemed to amplify the threat signal his body was sending. The more he tried not to think about the ambush, the more his nervous system seemed convinced that danger was present. His concentration at work suffered—he managed social media content for a nonprofit, a job that required sustained focus and creativity, but he found himself unable to hold a thought for more than a few minutes. His mind would fracture, pulled back to the dusty road, to the sound of Amara's breathing when she returned. He would start a caption for an Instagram post and lose the thread entirely, his eyes scanning the office windows instead. His supervisor had begun asking if everything was all right.

To manage the intrusive vigilance, Kofi had developed a strange distance from his own memories. He could describe the ambush in clinical detail—the time, the location, the sequence of events—but when he spoke about it, it felt as though he were reporting on something that had happened to someone else. The emotional truth of it, the fear and the shame, remained sealed off. This detachment quieted the memories temporarily, but it also meant that nothing felt real anymore, including his marriage. Zainab would reach for his hand and he would feel present only in body. The dissociation kept the threat at bay, but it also kept him isolated, adrift in his own life. His wife had stopped asking him to talk about what had happened. She had simply stopped asking him much of anything.

Kofi had finally sought help because Zainab had given him an ultimatum, delivered not in anger but in exhaustion. "I can't live with a ghost," she had said. He sat in the intake appointment understanding, with a clarity that surprised him, that he was trapped in a cycle he could not break alone—that his conviction of his own unreliability had made him hypervigilant, that his hypervigilance had made him retreat into detachment, and that his detachment had only deepened his sense that he was fundamentally broken and could not be trusted with anything that mattered. What frightened him most was that she might be right.
